IV.1.title: Choosing a neighbourhood
IV.1.reflection: It is humaneness that makes a neighbourhood beautiful. Someone who chooses a place to live without regard to it can hardly be called wise. Book IV, the book of ren, opens with the company one keeps as a place.
IV.1.question: What makes the place you live good or poor, apart from its buildings?

IV.2.title: At rest in ren
IV.2.reflection: Without ren a person cannot bear hardship long, nor enjoy good times long either. The humane rest in it; the wise find it profitable. Two kinds of goodness are distinguished: one that is at home in itself and one that sees its advantage.
IV.2.question: Is your goodness more often at rest, or more often calculating its benefit?

IV.3.title: Who can love and hate
IV.3.reflection: Only the humane person can truly love others and truly dislike them. The claim is not that the good love everyone; it is that their likes and dislikes are not bent by self-interest, so they can be trusted.
IV.3.question: Whose approval would you trust because you know it is not bent by their interest?

IV.4.title: A will set on ren
IV.4.reflection: If the will is truly set on humaneness, there will be no wickedness. The chapter places the decisive moment in the direction of the will, before any action.
IV.4.question: What is your will set on, today, before anything else?

IV.5.title: Not for the space of a meal
IV.5.reflection: Wealth and rank are what everyone wants, but not if they come the wrong way; poverty and low station are what everyone dislikes, but not to be escaped the wrong way. The junzi does not leave ren even for the length of a meal, in haste or in danger. Goodness is not a mood but a place one does not leave.
IV.5.question: In what kind of haste do you most easily leave your own standards?

IV.6.title: Strength enough for one day
IV.6.reflection: Confucius says he has never seen anyone who truly loved ren or truly hated what is not ren. Yet who has ever applied their strength to it for one day and found the strength lacking? He has not seen it. The demand is high and the door is open at the same time.
IV.6.question: What would one whole day of trying look like for you?
IV.6.exercise: Pick one hour today and give it fully to treating others well, then notice whether your strength ran out.

IV.7.title: Faults by kind
IV.7.reflection: A person's faults are of a piece with the kind of person they are. Look at the faults and you will know the goodness. A generous person errs by giving too much, a careful one by holding back; the fault shows the character it comes from.
IV.7.question: What does your most frequent fault say about what you value?

IV.8.title: In the morning, the Way
IV.8.reflection: To hear the Way in the morning and die in the evening would be enough. It is the most quoted line of the book about how much the Way is worth. It does not say what the Way is; it says what it would be worth to know it.
IV.8.question: What would you be content to have understood, if you understood nothing else?

IV.9.title: Ashamed of poor clothes
IV.9.reflection: A scholar who is set on the Way but ashamed of shabby clothes and plain food is not worth talking with. The chapter catches a contradiction: someone who claims a higher aim and is still measuring themselves by appearance.
IV.9.question: Where are you still measuring yourself by appearance, while saying you care about something else?

IV.10.title: No fixed for or against
IV.10.reflection: In the world the junzi has nothing he must do and nothing he must refuse; he goes with what is right, yi. The chapter rejects both rigid rules and drifting. The measure is not a list of positions but rightness in the case.
IV.10.question: What position do you hold out of habit rather than because it is right here?

IV.11.title: Virtue or comfort
IV.11.reflection: The junzi thinks of virtue, the small man of land and comfort; the junzi thinks of the law, the small man of favours. What a person thinks about, the chapter says, shows which of the two they are.
IV.11.question: What did you think about most today?

IV.12.title: Acting for profit
IV.12.reflection: One who acts always with an eye to profit will be much resented. Twelve words in Legge, and the observation is social more than moral: people notice, and they keep count.
IV.12.question: When did you resent someone for always looking to their own advantage, and did they know?

IV.13.title: Ritual and yielding
IV.13.reflection: If a state can be governed by ritual and deference, what difficulty is there? If not, what use is ritual? Legge's "complaisance" is the Chinese rang, yielding, giving way to others. Ritual that does not include yielding is not really ritual.
IV.13.question: Where would a little giving way make something easier?

IV.14.title: Worthy to be known
IV.14.reflection: Do not worry about having no position; worry about being fit for one. Do not worry about being unknown; seek to be worth knowing. The book turns the same worry around for the second time.
IV.14.question: If no one noticed your work for a year, would you still do it the same way?

IV.15.title: One thread
IV.15.reflection: Confucius tells Zeng Shen that his Way has one thread running through it, and leaves. The other disciples ask what he meant, and Zeng says: zhong and shu, doing one's utmost and measuring others by oneself, nothing more. Legge renders the pair as "true to the principles of our nature and the benevolent exercise of them to others". Whether Zeng's summary is the Master's is something the chapter leaves to the reader.
IV.15.question: If your own life has one thread, what would you name it?

IV.16.title: Right and profit
IV.16.reflection: The junzi understands what is right; the small man understands what pays. The line is about what each person is fluent in, what their mind turns to without effort.
IV.16.question: Which language are you more fluent in, what is right or what pays?

IV.17.title: Equal them, examine yourself
IV.17.reflection: When you see someone worthy, think of becoming their equal; when you see someone unworthy, look inward and examine yourself. Both encounters are turned into work on oneself. Neither ends in envy or contempt.
IV.17.question: Whom did you meet recently who could serve as either kind of mirror?
IV.17.exercise: The next time someone irritates you today, ask whether you share the fault, before you judge it.

IV.18.title: Remonstrating gently
IV.18.reflection: In serving parents, a child may object, but gently. If they will not listen, the child keeps respectful and does not give up, and does not complain even when it is hard. This is a description of conduct in the society of the time, where the child's place was below the parent's; the chapter asks for persistence and respect together, not for silence.
IV.18.question: How do you disagree with someone you also respect?

IV.19.title: A known address
IV.19.reflection: While parents are alive, a son does not travel far, and if he does travel, he must have a fixed destination. In a world without letters that arrived quickly, a parent's worry needed somewhere to rest. It is advice from a time of slow roads.
IV.19.question: Who would worry if they did not know where you were, and do they know?

IV.20.title: Three years, again
IV.20.reflection: The second half of I.11 returns almost word for word: if for three years a son does not change his father's way, he may be called filial. The repetition is one sign that the book was gathered from several sources rather than composed in one sitting.
IV.20.question: What do you think the compilers meant by keeping a repeated saying twice?

IV.21.title: Your parents' ages
IV.21.reflection: One must know the ages of one's parents, with joy that they have reached them and with fear that they are growing old. Two feelings for one fact. The chapter asks for attention more than for any action.
IV.21.question: How old are the people you love most, and what do you feel when you count the years?

IV.22.title: Words that outrun deeds
IV.22.reflection: The ancients were slow to speak because they were ashamed when their actions did not keep up with their words. Shame here is not humiliation but a sense of proportion between saying and doing.
IV.22.question: What have you announced that your actions have not yet caught up with?

IV.23.title: Restraint
IV.23.reflection: Those who hold themselves in check seldom go wrong. Legge's "the cautious seldom err" is the shortest saying in the book. It praises restraint, not timidity.
IV.23.question: Where would a moment's restraint have spared you trouble this week?

IV.24.title: Slow to speak, quick to act
IV.24.reflection: The junzi wishes to be hesitant in speech and quick in action. The same thought appears in II.13 and IV.22, in different words. It is one of the book's steadiest themes.
IV.24.question: Would the people who know you describe you as slow to speak or quick to speak?

IV.25.title: Virtue has neighbours
IV.25.reflection: Virtue, de, is never alone; it will have neighbours. Goodness attracts its own company, sooner or later. The chapter is a comfort for anyone who feels isolated in trying.
IV.25.question: Who has been a neighbour to your better self?

IV.26.title: Too many reproofs
IV.26.reflection: Ziyou observes that frequent remonstrance with a ruler leads to disgrace, and frequent reproof of a friend leads to distance. Even right correction has a measure. The book of ren ends with a limit on being right.
IV.26.question: Whom have you corrected too often?
